title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 About the workshop
Open and reproducible science helps others understand, evaluate, reuse, and extend research. In this 90-minute workshop, we follow one prepared R project from its source data to an archived result. We use HealthWellbeing to pool published correlations between health and well-being. Teaching dataset
The workshop is presented by James Bristow, Massey University, with co-author Hana Liang, Bioeconomy Science Institute.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Learning objectives
By the end of the workshop, participants should be able to:

Explain how the tools support different parts of a reproducible research workflow.
Describe dataset variables, provenance, licensing, and access conditions using a codebook and structured FAIR metadata.
Store a dataset with pins and retrieve a specific version.
Trace a result through a targets pipeline and a Quarto report.
Identify the files and metadata needed for a citable archive.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Building a connected workflow

Track changes with Git and review a change on GitHub. Version control and collaboration
Record R dependencies with renv and inspect the wider environment captured by Docker. Computational environments
Describe variables with codebook and record dataset metadata with dataspice. Dataset documentation and FAIR metadata
Store the full dataset and a teaching subset with pins, then retrieve a specific version. Dataset storage and versioning
Run the correlation meta-analysis with targets and inspect what rebuilds when the dataset version changes. Analytical pipelines
Render and inspect the analysis report in Quarto. Reporting and publishing
Find and cite a specific archive version on Zenodo. Research archiving

Together, these tools support a workflow whose history, dependencies, analytical steps, and outputs can be inspected and reused by other researchers.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Optional closing examples
The final five minutes include discussion and brief demonstrations if time allows. synthpop illustrates synthetic study summaries and vetiver shows how to link model versions to their training data. Optional extras and concluding discussion

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.5 Reproducibility when data cannot be shared
text:
1.5 Reproducibility when data cannot be shared
Open science can include restricted-access data. Researchers can document their methods, code, and access conditions while restricting the original observations.
Synthetic data can help readers test whether a workflow runs. Verifying findings based on original observations requires access to those observations. A differential privacy claim requires a validated mechanism and privacy accounting. NIST’s introduction to differentially private synthetic data

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.6 Principles to put into practice
Throughout the session, consider whether another researcher could:

Understand the purpose of the project and follow the analysis decisions.
Reproduce the environment and rerun the workflow on another machine.
Audit the history of changes and the relationship between inputs and outputs.
Trace a reported result to the versions of its data, fitted model, and software environment.
Reuse and extend the code and materials with clear documentation and licensing.
Assess sharing limits and distinguish a runnable workflow from verification of restricted-data findings.
Find and cite a preserved version of the research outputs.

We will consider common barriers to these goals, including undocumented dependencies, manual analysis steps, and assumptions tied to a single computing environment.

14.1.1 Abstract / description
Open and reproducible science is increasingly important for ensuring that research can be understood, evaluated, reused, and extended by others. This workshop provides a practical introduction to building open and reproducible research workflows using R and open-source tools. Participants will develop a workflow integrating GitHub, renv, Docker, targets, Quarto, and Zenodo. Rather than focusing primarily on the technical details of individual tools, the workshop will demonstrate how these tools can work together to support reproducibility throughout the research lifecycle.
renv helps manage software dependencies, Docker captures the computational environment, and targets provides a structured framework for organising and reproducing analytical workflows. Quarto connects code, analysis, results, and narrative into reproducible reports, while GitHub supports version control, collaboration, and open sharing. Finally, Zenodo provides a mechanism for preserving and archiving research outputs and assigning persistent identifiers.
The workshop will emphasise the principles underlying open and reproducible science: making research workflows transparent, portable, auditable, reusable, and accessible beyond the original researcher or computing environment. Participants will gain practical experience developing a workflow that can be shared, reproduced, and archived, while considering common barriers to reproducibility and strategies for addressing them.

title: 17  Accessibility
text:
17.1 Accessibility goals
For web content and interfaces, we work toward WCAG 2.2 Level AA. This is a development goal; any claim of conformance must be supported by an evaluation that identifies its scope, date, methods, findings, and remaining limitations.
Across the project, we prioritise:

title: 17  Accessibility
text:
Clear language, descriptive links, and a logical content structure.
Keyboard access and visible focus for interactive interfaces.
Meaningful labels, headings, and semantics for assistive technologies.
Readable content that works with zoom, different screen sizes, and user settings.
Equivalent ways to understand information presented through images, colour, audio, video, or interaction.
Clear instructions, actionable errors, and accessible examples and outputs.

title: 17  Accessibility
text:
17.2 Contributor expectations
Consider accessibility when adding or changing user-facing content or behaviour. Apply these practices where relevant:

Use a logical heading hierarchy, semantic lists, and descriptive link text.
Provide useful alternative text for informative images. For complex figures, include a nearby explanation or an accessible table of the relevant data. See the W3C alternative-text decision tree.
Give tables appropriate headers and explain units, abbreviations, and symbols.
Use sufficient contrast and additional cues alongside colour to convey meaning.
Provide captions for video and transcripts for audio, with descriptions of essential visual information where needed.
Keep text and controls usable with zoom and on narrow screens.
Give controls accessible names and states. Keep focus order logical, make actions work with a keyboard, and avoid keyboard traps.
Declare the language of web content and identify changes of language when needed.
Make instructions, code examples, command-line help, and error messages clear and usable without relying solely on screenshots or visual layout.


17.2.1 Reviewing changes
Use existing project checks where available. For affected interfaces, combine automated checks with manual keyboard testing and, where possible, checks with assistive technology. Automated tools cover only part of an accessibility review.
In a pull request, describe what was checked, the tools and environments used, any barriers found, and any checks that could not be completed. Record unresolved issues and workarounds so maintainers can assess their impact. Introduce or change automated checks through the project’s normal contribution process.

title: 17  Accessibility
text:
17.3 Reporting an accessibility barrier
Open an issue in the repository’s issue tracker. Use an accessibility template or label if one is available; a general issue is also welcome. If the tracker is unavailable or difficult to use, use a contact or support route documented in the repository’s README.
Include whatever information you can comfortably provide:

The task you were trying to complete and the barrier you encountered.
The affected page, file, command, feature, or output, including a version if known.
Steps to reproduce the problem and what you expected to happen.
Relevant browser, operating system, device, or assistive technology details.
The impact on your work and any workaround you have found.

Screenshots and recordings are optional. You do not need to disclose a disability, diagnosis, or other personal information to report a barrier or request help. Avoid including confidential data or credentials in a public report.

title: 17  Accessibility
text:
17.4 Prioritisation and response
Repository maintainers coordinate accessibility work and may delegate individual issues to contributors. Reports should be acknowledged respectfully and assessed according to their effect on users’ ability to complete tasks.
Prioritise barriers that prevent essential tasks or have no practical workaround. Consider the number of affected users, available alternatives, dependencies, and the effort needed to address an issue. Reporters do not need to assign a severity.
Track agreed next steps and, where possible, provide workarounds and progress updates. Set response or resolution targets only when the project can support them, and communicate changes to an agreed timeline. Invite feedback on whether a proposed fix resolves the reported barrier.

title: 17  Accessibility
text:
17.5 Tested environments and known limitations
Record the browsers, devices, assistive technologies, software versions, and output formats actually checked in project documentation, issues, or pull requests. Describe the scope and date of testing when reporting compatibility.
Document confirmed barriers with their user impact, affected versions, known workarounds, and follow-up work. Identify relevant limits in third-party tools or embedded content. Revisit these records as the project and its dependencies change.

title: 17  Accessibility
text:
17.6 Maintaining this policy
Maintainers should review this policy when user-facing features, support routes, or accessibility practices change. Suggestions and corrections are welcome through the repository’s usual contribution and support channels.

title: 19  AI-assisted development policy
text:
19.1 Responsibility and review
Contributors remain responsible for the accuracy and suitability of the work they submit. AI-generated contributions follow the same review and acceptance process as other contributions. A human contributor must take responsibility for the submission and complete any human review required by the project.
State whether human review is complete or pending. Agent-run checks and automated reviews provide evidence for reviewers; they do not constitute human review.

title: 19  AI-assisted development policy
text:
19.2 Agent scope and authorisation
Agents may implement assigned tasks, run appropriate checks, prepare changes, and carry out other actions covered by the contributor’s instructions. Follow repository-specific guidance, including agent instructions, contribution rules, and security policies where these are provided.
Respect the task’s scope and preserve existing work. A review-only request does not authorise edits. Keep unrelated changes separate, and identify assumptions or missing information that materially affect the work.
Commits, external messages, merges, deployments, releases, and other shared changes must follow the contributor’s authorisation and the project’s approval process. Existing authorisation applies to actions within its scope. Do not infer permission to perform unrelated or destructive actions from access to a tool.

title: 19  AI-assisted development policy
text:
19.3 Disclosing material AI assistance
Disclose material AI assistance where the work is submitted, such as a pull request description, issue, review, or other contribution record. Briefly state:

Which tool or service was used and what it helped produce or review.
Which checks were performed and their results.
Remaining limitations and whether human review is complete or pending.

For example: “An AI coding assistant helped implement the change. Unit tests pass; integration testing and human review are pending.”
Keep disclosure relevant to the contribution. Full chat transcripts, prompts, and large blocks of raw output are not required. Review any material shared publicly for confidential information or credentials.

title: 19  AI-assisted development policy
text:
19.4 Verification and evidence
Check generated code, explanations, references, and API usage against the project’s actual environment and appropriate sources. Do not invent results, citations, provenance, test outcomes, or security and privacy guarantees. Distinguish proposed work from implemented and verified behaviour.
Run checks appropriate to the change. Report failures, skipped checks, missing dependencies, and untested environments accurately. Syntax checks, tests, builds, rendered documents, and executed workflows provide different evidence; identify which checks actually ran and what they establish.
For work involving data, models, or analytical results, preserve source inputs and record the versions, parameters, transformations, and environment needed to understand or reproduce the result. Explain substantive assumptions and use appropriate validation for the project’s domain.
Keep dependency changes deliberate and review generated files and configuration for effects beyond the assigned task. Follow the project’s established testing, formatting, accessibility, and review practices.

title: 19  AI-assisted development policy
text:
19.5 Data protection and confidentiality
Use only data and services approved for the task. Share the minimum context needed, and check applicable organisational rules, data-owner permissions, and service settings before providing non-public material to an external AI service.
Do not expose credentials, personal information, confidential code, or restricted data through prompts, logs, generated examples, or contribution records. Use public, synthetic, or redacted examples where appropriate, and verify that the chosen example is suitable for sharing.

title: 19  AI-assisted development policy
text:
19.6 Licensing and provenance
Respect software licences, copyright, and attribution requirements when using AI-generated material or adapting suggested code and text. Verify source and licensing information when it affects whether an output can be included. Preserve required notices and document relevant sources or adaptations.

title: 19  AI-assisted development policy
text:
19.7 Contributions and concerns
Follow the repository’s contribution and conduct policies where available. Report suspected vulnerabilities or disclosures of sensitive information through the project’s documented security or private reporting route. Use the normal support or issue channels for other questions about AI-assisted contributions.
Maintainers should update this policy as the project’s tools, risks, and review practices change. Project-specific requirements may supplement this policy and should be documented alongside it.

title: 4  Preparation
text:
4.1 Learning objectives
Before the timed session, you should be able to open the workshop project, identify its source data, and load a verified copy in R. You will use the same project and dataset throughout the workshop.
Allow time for downloads and setup before the session. Some familiarity with R is helpful; you do not need previous experience with meta-analysis.

title: 4  Preparation
text:
4.2 Our teaching dataset
We use HealthWellbeing from section 4.2.4, Correlations, of Doing Meta-Analysis with R: A Hands-On Guide. It contains study-level summaries of the association between health and well-being. It is also distributed with the dmetar package.
The original review is Ngamaba, Panagioti, and Armitage (2017). Consult the dataset documentation for the variable definitions and original reference.
We will download the authors’ data file directly, so these opening activities do not require installation of dmetar. Keep the raw file unchanged and record its source separately from any transformations you make later.

title: 4  Preparation
text:
4.3 Choose your computing environment
Use one of these routes:

Local R: install R and an editor such as RStudio. The reference environment uses R 4.4.1. Record any difference if you use another version.
Docker: use the workshop RStudio image confirmed by the instructor. Follow the Docker instructions before the session; downloading an image can take time.

Both routes need Git for the local version-control activity. A GitHub account lets you practise sharing from your own fork. Install Quarto before the session if you will render reports locally later; HTML reporting does not require LaTeX.
Browser-based Binder access is still being prepared. Use a verified local or Docker environment for this workshop.

title: 4  Preparation
text:
4.4 Workshop packages
The committed renv.lock records the packages for the workshop, including knitr and rmarkdown for rendering and synthpop and vetiver for the optional exercises. On Linux, building the dataspice dependency jqr from source needs the jq development library.
Run the lesson chunks in the R Console. Use Quarto with knitr and rmarkdown when you are ready to render the standalone report.

title: 4  Preparation
text:
4.5 Get your own project copy

Open the workshop repository and use Fork to create a copy in your GitHub account.
In your fork, select Code, copy its HTTPS clone URL, and clone it with Git. Replace YOUR-USERNAME below with your GitHub username.

git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.git
cd open-and-reproducible-science-in-r
Open open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.Rproj in RStudio. For Docker, open the project in the mounted checkout described in the environment chapter. Keep terminal commands and R Console commands rooted in this project directory.
The project’s .Rprofile activates renv; first startup may download renv. Restore the project library in the R Console before the session or before rendering locally. Repeat this step after updating renv.lock.
renv::restore()
Check your R version and the state of the restored library.

title: 4  Preparation
section: 4.6 Download and verify the raw data
text:
4.6 Download and verify the raw data
Run the following in the R Console from the project root. The R chunks are also configured to run during rendering; setup chunks are uncached and other R chunks use the cache.
The download comes from the resource linked in the book. The checksum identifies the exact file used to prepare these lessons. If you already have a different copy, keep it and ask the instructor to resolve the difference.

raw_file <- file.path("data", "raw", "healthwellbeing.rda")
source_url <- paste0(
  "https://www.protectlab.org/meta-analysis-in-r/data/",
  "healthwellbeing.rda"
)

dir.create(dirname(raw_file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
if (!file.exists(raw_file)) {
  download.file(source_url, destfile = raw_file, mode = "wb")
}

expected_md5 <- "0d74964b0b7168379a2b015cb648b326"
actual_md5 <- unname(tools::md5sum(raw_file))
stopifnot(identical(actual_md5, expected_md5))
actual_md5

[1] "0d74964b0b7168379a2b015cb648b326"


Load into a separate environment so the file does not silently replace objects in your working session. Use an explicit name for the dataset you will inspect.

data_env <- new.env(parent = baseenv())
loaded_names <- load(raw_file, envir = data_env)
stopifnot(identical(loaded_names, "HealthWellbeing"))
health <- data_env[["HealthWellbeing"]]

expected_columns <- c("author", "cor", "n", "population", "country")
stopifnot(
  is.data.frame(health),
  nrow(health) == 29L,
  identical(names(health), expected_columns),
  !anyNA(health),
  all(is.finite(health$cor)),
  all(abs(health$cor) < 1),

5.1 Learning objectives

title: 5  Open and reproducible science
text:
5.2 Why this matters
A reported result is easier to evaluate when its data, analytical decisions, code, and software environment can be traced. Sharing code helps, but the code also needs identifiable inputs and instructions that work beyond its author’s current R session.
In this workshop, reproducibility means being able to rerun a documented workflow with its specified inputs and environment. Open science also concerns how methods and outputs can be inspected, accessed, and reused. Reproducibility does not establish that the scientific assumptions are correct, and openness still needs to respect licences and access conditions.

text:
5.3 Our example: health and well-being
The teaching question is: What association between health and well-being is reported across the included studies? We use the HealthWellbeing example from section 4.2.4 of the guide.
Each row is a study summary, not a participant record. The columns are:

8.1 Introduction
We will describe the HealthWellbeing dataset so a collaborator can interpret the five columns and find the original teaching file. By the end of these 12 minutes, you should be able to read a data dictionary and explain what the dataset metadata adds.
FAIR stands for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. An identifiable source helps people find the data. Access instructions explain how to obtain it. Structured metadata helps software interpret it. Definitions, provenance, and reuse terms help people work out whether the data suit their question. Access can have conditions. 10.1 Introduction
We will run a targets pipeline that reads a specified HealthWellbeing version, pools the study correlations, and writes a summary for the report. By the end of these 18 minutes, you should be able to trace the summary back to its input and predict what rebuilds when you select another version.
You need Git and box, pins, targets, and meta in your workshop environment. The dependency graph also uses visNetwork. Start with your Git checkout, local board, and version selection file. Your instructor can share a prepared board and summary for comparison. Dataset storage and versioning

title: 10  Reproducible analytical pipelines
text:
10.2 Inspect the pipeline
The script is pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R. Open it in your editor and follow the data dependencies in this order.
version_file -> data_version -> dataset_file -> studies -> fit
fit, data_version -> result -> summary_file
We mark the selector, pinned RDS, and summary CSV as file targets. At fitting time, the pipeline records the Git revision, the script checksum, and whether the script has local changes. If you work with local edits, keep a copy of that script to reproduce the fit.
The model uses the raw Pearson correlations and study sample sizes. Meta transforms each correlation to Fisher’s z scale and pools the effects with a random-effects model. We use restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to estimate between-study variance and the Hartung–Knapp method for the 95% interval. The summary converts the estimate and limits back to the correlation scale.
This model treats study summaries as independent and assumes their correlations address a comparable association. Differences in populations, measures, and sampling limit interpretation. This is a worked example of pooling reported effects from the supplied studies. Section 4.2.4 of the guide

text:
13.4 Model versioning
We will use vetiver and pins to store two illustrative linear regressions under the same model name. The second adds log sample size as a predictor. Both regressions give each study equal weight and serve to illustrate model versioning. The core meta-analysis uses study precision and between-study variance when pooling effects.
Reuse the local model board across renders and keep the version identifiers for each pair of fits. Cached model chunks reuse their recorded identifiers. Refreshing the cache fits a new pair and retains earlier versions in the board. Keep the board with its document cache; if you remove the board, refresh the cache when rendering again.

box::use(
  pins[pin_exists, pin_versions],
  stats[lm],
  vetiver[vetiver_model, vetiver_pin_write, vetiver_pin_read]
)

model_board <- board_folder(
  file.path(workshop_dir, "model_store"),
  versioned = TRUE
)
model_name <- "health_wellbeing"

code_revision <- system2("git", c("rev-parse", "HEAD"), stdout = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(code_revision) == 1L, grepl("^[0-9a-f]{40}$", code_revision))
model_source <- list(
  data_version = full_version,
  code_revision = code_revision,
  r_version = as.character(getRversion()),
  vetiver_version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("vetiver"))
)


previous_versions <- if (pin_exists(model_board, model_name)) {
  pin_versions(model_board, model_name)$version
} else {
  character()
}

model_v1 <- lm(z ~ population, data = original)
v1 <- vetiver_model(
  model_v1,
  model_name = model_name,
  description = "Illustrative regression on population.",
  metadata = model_source
)
vetiver_pin_write(model_board, v1)
first_version <- setdiff(
  pin_versions(model_board, model_name)$version, previous_versions
)
stopifnot(length(first_version) == 1L)

model_v2 <- lm(z ~ population + log_n, data = original)
v2 <- vetiver_model(
  model_v2,
  model_name = model_name,
  description = "Illustrative regression on population and log sample size.",
  metadata = model_source
)
vetiver_pin_write(model_board, v2)

model_history <- pin_versions(model_board, model_name)
second_version <- setdiff(
  model_history$version, c(previous_versions, first_version)
)
stopifnot(length(first_version) == 1L, length(second_version) == 1L)
